newsitem.title: UK: Sterling debt and futures closing report.
newsitem.headline: Sterling debt and futures closing report.

text.p: Gilts ended marginally in the black on Wednesday but that proved to be a disappointing display given a well-covered auction and a robust, but not startling set of retail sales figures.
The June gilt future settled 2/32 higher at 109-15, well below its 109-25 session high. Dealers said weak U.S. T-bond futures proved difficult to shake off.

A trader at a U.S. bank said the Bank of England's five-year gilt auction, although it was covered 3.49 times, had not been bought by client investors en masse. Instead, the big City houses were forced to pick it up.

"That has become more apparent as the day has gone on. The five-year part of the curve has underperformed Germany, as you would expect," he said. The five-year gilt/Bund spread edged out by two basis points from Tuesday.
"The U.S. market hasn't helped either," the trader said. June U.S. T-bond futures were 6/32 lower at 107-30 by 1520 GMT.

On top of that, a 0.3 percent rise in March UK retail sales, leaving them 4.0 percent up on the year, and evidence from the Confederation of British Industry showing domestic manufacturing orders rising at their fastest in two years, suggested the economy needs reigning in.
"The economic data were really not supportive of gilts," the trader said.
The CBI said the economy needed either a rate rise, but more desirably a fiscal tightening to cool it down. An International Monetary Fund report issued later, echoed that sentiment.
The IMF said Britain needed an early interest rate rise and some fiscal tightening to cool domestic demand.

"With signs consumers are growing less price sensitive and our expectation that retail sales growth will pick up to around 5.0 percent this year, this is not good news for inflation," said Adam Cole, UK economist at James Capel.
Minutes from the March 5 monetary meeting between Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke and Bank of England Governor Eddie George showed the latter still pressing for a quarter-point rate rise.
But Clarke said it was impossible to ignore the deflationary implications of sterling's rise and said that consumer demand was growing at a sustainable rate.

Kevin Adams, gilts analyst at BZW, said assuming Labour wins the election clearly and interest rates are put up soon after, gilts could be due a rally. "We saw massive curve flattening late last year. That could soon be back on the agenda."
June short sterling settled one basis point lower at 93.38, discounting a half-point rate rise by the end of the first half.
An opinion poll out early on Wednesday, showing Labour's lead cut to five points from 14, briefly focused the market back on the election. But most traders dismissed it as a one-off.
"It was generally regarded as a rogue poll. As long as Labour get a workable majority, the market will be comfortable with that," the U.S. bank trader said.
Elections are just eight days away. The trader said gilts would tread a narrow range until then.
